title: Document and Content Management

toc.title: Ontology vs. Taxonomy vs. Data Model

html:
1Definition and Goals

Definition: Planning, implementation, and control activities for lifecycle management of data and information found in any form or medium.

Focus: Controlling capture, storage, access, and use of data stored outside relational databases — unstructured and semi-structured information.

Statistic: Estimated 80% of all stored data is maintained outside relational databases (unstructured). More than 90% of documents created today are electronic.

3 Goals:

  1. Comply with legal obligations and customer expectations regarding records management
  2. Ensure effective and efficient storage, retrieval, and use of documents and content
  3. Ensure integration capabilities between structured and unstructured content

2Business Drivers

  • Regulatory compliance — organizations must maintain records of certain activities
  • E-discovery — ability to respond to litigation; finding electronic records for legal proceedings
  • Business continuity — vital records management for disaster recovery
  • Efficiency — manage workflow, collaboration, locate documents faster, prevent document loss

E-discovery Law (US): US Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (FRCP) governed discovery since 1938; 2006 amendments accommodated Electronically Stored Information (ESI).

3ARMA Generally Accepted Recordkeeping Principles (GARP) — 2009

Source: ARMA International — not-for-profit professional association for records and information management.

8 GARP Principles:

Principle Description
Accountability Assign senior executive; adopt policies; ensure auditability
Integrity Records have reasonable guarantee of authenticity and reliability
Protection Reasonable protection for personal or otherwise protected information
Compliance Comply with applicable laws and binding authorities
Availability Maintain information enabling timely, efficient, accurate retrieval
Retention Retain information appropriate time (operational, legal, regulatory, fiscal requirements)
Disposition Secure and appropriate disposition per policies and law
Transparency Document policies, processes, and activities; available to staff and stakeholders

ARMA Maturity Model — 5 Levels:

  1. Sub-Standard — concerns not addressed or minimally
  2. In Development — developing recognition of impact
  3. Essential — minimum requirements met for legal/regulatory compliance
  4. Proactive — program established with continuous improvement focus
  5. Transformational — integrated into corporate infrastructure and business processes

4Key Concepts: Content

Content vs. Document

  • A Document is to Content what a bucket is to water — a container
  • Content = the data and information inside the file, document, or website

Content Metadata

Essential for managing unstructured data; without Metadata, impossible to inventory and organize content.

Content Modeling

Converting logical content concepts into content types, attributes, and data types with relationships.

  • Attribute — describes something specific about the content
  • Data type — restricts type of data an attribute may hold

Three Content Delivery System Types

Type Description
Push Delivery Content delivered on predetermined schedule; syndication; RSS (Really Simple Syndication)
Pull Delivery Users pull content through Internet; example: online retail stores
Interactive Exchange of real-time data; uses EAI, CDC, data integration

5Controlled Vocabularies

Definition: A defined list of explicitly allowed terms used to index, categorize, tag, sort, and retrieve content.

Standard: ANSI/NISO Z39.19-2005 — guidelines for Construction, Format, and Management of Monolingual Controlled Vocabularies.

Folksonomies: Bottom-up classification — terms obtained through social tagging by users (not authoritative).

Types of Controlled Vocabularies (Simplest to Most Complex)

Type Key Facts
Term / Pick Lists Just lists; no relationships; reduce domain of values; pick lists on UI
Synonym Rings Set of terms with equivalent meaning; users searching one term find all related content; manual development
Authority Lists One preferred term; others are variants; cross-references guide user from non-preferred to preferred
Taxonomies Naming structure with controlled vocabulary; hierarchical or other structure; enables navigation
Thesauri Most complex; combines synonym lists + taxonomies; hierarchical + associative + equivalent relationships
Ontologies Represents concepts and relationships; used in Semantic Web; open-world assumption

5 Taxonomy Structure Types

Type Description
Flat No relationships; all categories equal; e.g., list of countries
Hierarchical Tree structure; at least two levels; moving up expands, moving down refines
Polyhierarchy Child nodes may have multiple parents; risk of invalid traversals
Facet Star structure; each node associated with center (object); facets = attributes of center object
Network Combines hierarchical + facet; any two nodes can link; e.g., recommender engines, thesauri

Three Term Relationship Types (ANSI/NISO Z39.19)

Type Description
Equivalent Two terms have same meaning; one preferred; most common in IT systems for data mapping
Hierarchical Broader (general) to narrower (specific); parent/child
Related Term Associatively but not hierarchically linked

6Documents and Records

Document

Electronic or paper objects containing instructions, requirements, or logs; examples: procedures, protocols, specifications.

Record

Only a subset of documents designated as records; provide evidence of actions taken and decisions made.

ISO 15489 — defines records management: "the field of management responsible for the efficient and systematic control of the creation, receipt, maintenance, use and disposition of records."

5 Record Types

  1. Physical — documents, memos, contracts, reports, microfiche
  2. Electronic — email content, attachments, instant messaging
  3. Website — content on websites
  4. Media/Hardware — documents on all types of media and hardware
  5. Database — data captured in databases

Vital Record

Type of record required to resume organization's operations in event of disaster.

Well-Prepared Records — 5 Characteristics

  1. Content — accurate, complete, truthful
  2. Context — descriptive Metadata (creator, date, relationships) collected at time of creation
  3. Timeliness — created promptly after event/action/decision
  4. Permanency — once designated as records, cannot be changed
  5. Structure — clear appearance; correct forms/templates; legible; consistent terminology

Digital Asset Management (DAM)

Similar to document management; focuses on rich media documents: video, logos, photographs.

7Three Control Levels (ANSI Standard 859)

Level Description Criteria
Formal Control Formal change initiation; thorough evaluation; full status accounting High criticality; significant project/enterprise impact
Revision Control Less formal; notifies stakeholders; increments versions Moderate criticality; change history needed
Custody Control Least formal; safe storage and retrieval only Low criticality; minimal impact

8E-discovery

Definition: Process of finding electronic records that might serve as evidence in a legal action.

ESI — Electronically Stored Information: All electronic data subject to discovery.

Data Map: Inventory of all ESI data sources, applications, and IT environments including owners, custodians, geographic locations, and data types.

EDRM — Electronic Discovery Reference Model (8 Phases)

Phase Key Activity
1. Identification Early Case Assessment + Early Data Assessment; interviews with records mgmt, data custodians, IT
2. Preservation Data placed in legal hold so it cannot be destroyed
3. Collection Transfer of identified data to legal counsel in legally defensible manner
4. Processing De-duplicate, search, analyze; determines what moves to Review
5. Review Documents selected for response; privileged documents withheld
6. Analysis Focuses on content; understand circumstances, facts, potential evidence
7. Production Data turned over to opposing counsel per agreed specifications
8. Presentation Displaying ESI at depositions, hearings, trials

ESI Production Formats:

  • Native Production — original file format
  • Near-native Production — altered through extraction/conversion
  • Image/Near Paper Format — produced as image
  • Fielded Data — Metadata extracted; produced as text-delimited or XML file

LHN (Legal Hold Notification): Identifying, locking, and notifying parties of data subject to legal hold.

9Ontology vs. Taxonomy vs. Data Model

Concept Key Distinction
Taxonomy Provides data content classifications for given concept area; closed-world assumption
Data Model Calls out entity, attribute, valid values; closed-world assumption
Ontology Entity, attribute, and content completely mixed; open-world assumption (what is not declared can still be true)

Ontology Languages:

  • RDFS (Resource Description Framework Schema) — encodes knowledge about specific domains
  • OWL (Web Ontology Language) — extension to RDFS; formal syntax for defining ontologies

W3C Semantic Web Standards:

  • RDF (Resource Description Framework) — common framework for describing web resources; stored in triplestore using SPARQL
  • SKOS (Simple Knowledge Organization System) — RDF vocabulary for hierarchical concept classification
  • Schema.org — open source semantic markup specification; enables rich snippets in search results

10Activities

Activity 1: Plan for Lifecycle Management

  • Define records; develop classification/indexing systems; develop taxonomies
  • Plan for records management (paper + electronic + structured)
  • Develop content strategy: assessment → strategy definition → recommendations

Activity 2: Create Content Handling Policies

Typical Policy Topics:

  1. Scope and compliance
  2. Vital records identification and protection
  3. Retention schedule
  4. Legal holds
  5. Storage requirements (onsite/offsite)
  6. Storage media management
  7. Email management
  8. Destruction methods

Additional Policy Areas: Social media, BYOD/BYOA/WYOD device access, sensitive data handling.

Activity 3: Manage the Lifecycle

  • Capture records (tag with minimum Metadata: ID, date/time, title/author)
  • Manage versioning using ANSI Standard 859 control levels
  • Backup and recovery (include in business continuity plan)
  • Retain and dispose per retention schedule
  • Risk of not removing data: older unpurged records discoverable for litigation

Activity 4: Publish and Deliver Content

  • Provide access via portal, search engines, internal search professionals
  • Deliver through acceptable channels; users want content on device of their choosing

11Tools

Enterprise Content Management (ECM)

May consist of platform components + applications; in-house or cloud-based.

Document Management System

  • Tracks and stores electronic documents; captures via scanners or OCR
  • Common capabilities: storage, versioning, security, Metadata management, content indexing, retrieval
  • OCR (Optical Character Recognition) — converts scanned text to computer-readable form
  • ICR (Intelligent Character Recognition) — advanced OCR; handles handwriting

Records Management System

  • Automates retention and disposition
  • Supports e-discovery, long-term archiving, vital records program

Content Management System (CMS)

  • Collects, organizes, indexes, retrieves content; web content management
  • Manages content through lifecycle; provides versioning and workflow

Markup and Exchange Formats

Format Key Facts
XML Extensible Markup Language; integrates structured + unstructured data; tags data elements; uses namespaces
JSON JavaScript Object Notation; lightweight; preferred for web/NoSQL; structures: objects + arrays
RDF Resource Description Framework; triples (subject-predicate-object); stored in triplestore; uses SPARQL
Schema.org Open source semantic markup; enables rich snippets in search

REST Technology: Can return either XML or JSON content.

TAR (Technology-Assisted Review)

  • Workflow for e-discovery document review
  • Uses predictive coding to sort remaining documents by relevancy

12Governance

Information Governance Reference Model (IGRM)

  • Shows relationship of Information Governance to organizational functions
  • Outer ring: stakeholders who create policies/tools/infrastructure
  • Center: lifecycle diagram
  • Complements ARMA's GARP

KPI Categories

Records Management KPIs:

  • Strategic: compliance with regulatory requirements, governance compliance
  • Operational: resources (costs), training, daily service delivery

E-discovery KPIs:

  • Cost reduction
  • Average time to turn around e-discovery requests (efficiency)
  • Speed of implementing Legal Hold Notification (LHN)

ECM KPIs:

  • Precision — proportion of retrieved documents that are actually relevant
  • Recall — proportion of all relevant documents that are actually retrieved
  • Storage utilization, search retrieval performance, cost reduction

13Practice Q&A

Q1: What is the definition of Document and Content Management? A: Planning, implementation, and control activities for lifecycle management of data and information found in any form or medium.

Q2: What percentage of stored data is estimated to be unstructured (outside relational databases)? A: Approximately 80%.

Q3: What are the 8 GARP principles? A: Accountability, Integrity, Protection, Compliance, Availability, Retention, Disposition, Transparency.

Q4: What is the difference between a document and a record? A: A document is any electronic or paper object; a record is a subset of documents specifically designated to provide evidence of business activities.

Q5: What is a Vital Record? A: A record required to resume organization's operations in the event of a disaster.

Q6: What are the 5 taxonomy structure types? A: Flat, Hierarchical, Polyhierarchy, Facet, Network.

Q7: What is EDRM and how many phases does it have? A: Electronic Discovery Reference Model — standards and guidelines for e-discovery; 8 phases.

Q8: What is the key legal context for e-discovery? A: US Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (FRCP) governed discovery since 1938; 2006 amendments accommodated ESI (Electronically Stored Information).

Q9: What is the open-world assumption and which concept uses it? A: Something not explicitly declared can still be true; used by Ontology (vs. closed-world assumption in taxonomy/data models).

Q10: What is RDF and how does it store data? A: Resource Description Framework — common framework for describing web resources; uses subject-predicate-object triples stored in a triplestore queried via SPARQL.

Q11: What are the 3 ANSI Standard 859 control levels? A: Formal Control (most stringent), Revision Control (moderate), Custody Control (least formal — storage and retrieval only).

Q12: What is a Legal Hold Notification (LHN)? A: Process of identifying data relevant to legal proceedings, locking it to prevent editing/deletion, and notifying all parties.

Q13: What is the difference between OCR and ICR? A: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) converts scanned printed text; ICR (Intelligent Character Recognition) is more advanced and can handle handwriting.

Q14: What is an Authority List? A: Controlled vocabulary where one term is preferred; others are variants; cross-references guide user from non-preferred to preferred term (e.g., US Library of Congress Subject Headings).

Q15: What are the ECM KPIs for information retrieval quality? A: Precision (proportion of retrieved documents that are relevant) and Recall (proportion of all relevant documents that are retrieved).

14Quick Reference

Concept Key Fact
Definition Lifecycle management of data in any form/medium
80% statistic Estimated data outside relational databases (unstructured)
3 Goals Legal compliance; effective storage/retrieval; integration with structured data
ARMA GARP 8 principles; published 2009
ARMA Maturity Levels 5 levels: Sub-Standard → Transformational
ISO 15489 Defines records management
ANSI/NISO Z39.19-2005 Controlled vocabulary guidelines
ANSI Standard 859 3 control levels: Formal, Revision, Custody
EDRM 8-phase e-discovery model
FRCP 1938 / 2006 Discovery since 1938; ESI amendments 2006
LHN Legal Hold Notification — lock and notify
Vital Record Required for operations after disaster
Controlled vocab types Term list → Synonym Ring → Authority List → Taxonomy → Thesaurus → Ontology
5 Taxonomy types Flat, Hierarchical, Polyhierarchy, Facet, Network
3 Term relationships Equivalent, Hierarchical, Related
Open-world assumption Ontology — undeclared facts can still be true
RDF Triplestore; subject-predicate-object; SPARQL query
Precision/Recall ECM retrieval quality KPIs
TAR Technology-Assisted Review for e-discovery
